metrics.label: Henry Hub gas

metrics.label: Coal API2 (ARA)

metrics.label: Heating oil / gasoil

metrics.label: RBOB gasoline

metrics.label: Dry bulk ETF (BDRY)

metrics.label: Baltic Capesize Index
metrics.blurb: The Capesize component of the Baltic Dry Index. The most volatile part, and effectively a bet on Chinese steel production.

metrics.label: Baltic Panamax Index
metrics.blurb: The Panamax component. Coal and grain rather than iron ore, so it follows harvests and power demand more than steel.

metrics.label: Baltic Supramax Index
metrics.blurb: The Supramax component. These ships have their own cranes and serve smaller ports, so it reflects broad trade rather than one commodity.

metrics.label: Baltic Dry Index

metrics.label: VLSFO Singapore

metrics.label: VLSFO Rotterdam

metrics.label: VLSFO Fujairah
metrics.blurb: The Middle East bunker hub, where most VLCC voyages refuel.

metrics.label: Diesel crack vs Brent

brief.text:
The clearest move in today's data is in bunkers — the fuel ships burn — where VLSFO (very low sulphur fuel oil, the main marine fuel) fell at all four major bunkering ports this morning: Singapore down 62.00 to 941.50 USD/t (-6.2%), Fujairah down 35.00 to 956.50, Houston down 34.00 to 780.00 and Rotterdam down 8.00 to 755.50 (-1.0%). That matters directly to anyone fixing a voyage, because bunkers are the largest single voyage cost and a cheaper bunker lifts the TCE — time charter equivalent, the daily earnings a voyage returns to the owner — at any given freight rate. Note the spread: Singapore and Fujairah remain far above Rotterdam and Houston, so where you stem fuel still changes your economics materially.

Crude barely moved today: Brent 103.74 USD/bbl, up 0.14 (+0.1%), WTI 96.19, up 0.10, with the Brent–WTI spread at 7.55 USD/bbl and the diesel crack at 87.13 USD/bbl. Gasoil was 4.54 USD/gal (+0.3%) and RBOB gasoline 2.95 USD/gal (+0.4%). The size of the bunker fall against a flat crude is not explained by anything in this data — I would not attach it to a headline. No freight benchmark has refreshed today. The Baltic Dry Index, which tracks dry bulk ship earnings, stood at 2,590 points on Tuesday 3 November, down 58 (-2.2%); the Panamax index was 1,866 and Supramax 1,846 on the same day. The Capesize index — Capesizes are the largest dry bulkers, mainly iron ore and coal — was 3,963 on Monday 2 November. The tanker ETF BWET was 835.00 on Tuesday 3 November, down 8.5%, with no explanation in today's data.

Hormuz developed today: a VLCC's engine room was struck in Omani waters, reported as the fifth confirmed attack in the first three days of November, and separate coverage describes a US–Iran economic standoff. Counter to that, October Hormuz crossings hit a three-month high despite the attacks, though VLCC traffic declined. The Black Sea drone attacks, Russian diesel export restrictions, the Los Angeles/Long Beach security-worker dispute with its 4 November deadline, and Chinese patrols off Taiwan all had no fresh news today and stand unchanged.

Watch two things. First, whether Baltic tanker TCEs refresh and how they sit against the fifth Hormuz attack — all current tanker figures are three to eight sessions old. Second, the Los Angeles/Long Beach deadline, which falls today and is unreported so far.

storylines.title: Direct attacks on ships in Hormuz
storylines.what: Attacks on commercial shipping in and around the Strait of Hormuz have continued into November, including a VLCC whose engine room was struck in Omani waters, reported as the fifth confirmed attack in the first three days of the month.
storylines.why_it_matters: Strikes on hulls raise war-risk premiums and crew-safety objections for Arabian Gulf liftings, shrinking the pool of willing owners and supporting crude and product tanker earnings.
storylines.latest: A VLCC engine room was struck in Omani waters, the fifth confirmed attack in the first three days of November; separate reporting describes a US-Iran standoff with Trump threatening renewed attacks against Iran.
sources: VLCC engine room struck in latest Hormuz attack

storylines.title: Hormuz and Bab al-Mandab transits and Gulf congestion
storylines.what: Strait of Hormuz traffic rose in October to its highest monthly level since July, supported by stronger dry bulk and LNG movements even as VLCC traffic declined. Red Sea traffic also rose. Vessel waiting remains elevated across the Arabian Gulf.
storylines.why_it_matters: Transit counts and waiting times show whether ships route through or around high-risk waters, changing voyage lengths, tonne-mile demand and effective fleet supply.
storylines.latest: October Hormuz crossings hit a three-month high despite the attacks, with dry bulk and LNG up but VLCC traffic down; Red Sea traffic also increased.
sources: Hormuz Oct crossings at 3-month high despite attacks, Red Sea traffic also rises

storylines.title: Drone attacks on shipping in the western Black Sea
storylines.what: A Greek container ship sank after being hit by naval drones off Bulgaria, the latest in a series of strikes in the western Black Sea.
storylines.why_it_matters: Attacks on ships and port infrastructure threaten grain and dry bulk loadings from the region and add insurance and routing costs for any vessel calling there.

storylines.title: Russian diesel flows and export restrictions
storylines.what: A reported US-Russia agreement on supplying extra diesel to the US market has met political opposition, while Russia has extended a general ban on most diesel exports until the end of January, with some volumes still allowed to flow.
storylines.why_it_matters: Diesel export restrictions and any reopened Atlantic route reshape clean product tanker ton-miles and MR and LR employment patterns.

storylines.title: Port labour disruption in the US and Europe
storylines.what: A contract standoff involving 250 security workers threatens to freeze operations across Los Angeles and Long Beach terminals after a 4 November deadline extension, while dockworkers struck across Europe and beyond over arms shipments through their ports.
storylines.why_it_matters: Labour action at container and ferry berths disrupts berthing schedules and cargo flows, and the unresolved US West Coast dispute leaves a large share of US import capacity exposed to stoppage.

storylines.title: Chinese patrols off Taiwan's east coast
storylines.what: Taiwan's Coast Guard says China's Coast Guard is harassing shipping with a patrol off Taiwan's east coast and asserting what Taipei calls a fictional jurisdiction, and has sent its own ships in response.
storylines.why_it_matters: Interference with commercial traffic near a major East Asian routing corridor can affect transit decisions, insurance and schedules for ships serving North Asia.
